en: The Waling-waling, known as the Queen of Philippine Orchids, grows high on mossy trees in the cloud forests of Mount Apo.
National Scientist Ramon Barba discovered that spraying mango trees with potassium nitrate solution induces them to flower abundantly.
The Philippine Eagle, our national bird, requires large, unbroken dipterocarp forests to hunt monkeys and build its massive nests.
Ifugao farmers maintain their famous rice terraces by channeling rainwater from protected mountain forests through stone-walled irrigation canals.
During Lucban's Pahiyas Festival, locals decorate houses with kiping, which are colorful leaf-shaped wafers made from ground rice.
The Narra, our national tree, has compound leaves that visibly fold together at night or during dry spells.
National Scientist Angel Alcala established marine sanctuaries in Apo Island to help damaged coral reefs visibly regenerate fish populations.
T'boli weavers extract strong abaca fibers from plant stalks to dye and weave the traditional T'nalak cloth.
The South Sea pearl, declared our national gem, is naturally produced by large Pinctada maxima oysters in Palawan waters.
Fishermen in coastal villages rely on the northeast monsoon, called amihan, to provide calm seas for safe boat navigation.
The carabao, our national animal, cools its body by wallowing in mud because it lacks functional sweat glands.
While exiled in Dapitan, Jose Rizal collected and studied hundreds of local beetle, snake, and seashell specimens.
